text_blocks.snippet: Immunotherapy is a type of cancer treatment that uses the body's own immune system to fight cancer cells. It works by either boosting the immune system's ability to recognize and attack cancer cells or by directly attacking cancer cells.
snippet_highlighted_words: uses the body's own immune system to fight cancer cells

list.title: Harnessing the immune system:
list.snippet: Immunotherapy aims to leverage the power of the immune system to target and destroy cancer cells.

list.title: Types of immunotherapy:
list.snippet: There are various forms of immunotherapy, including:
Immune checkpoint inhibitors: These drugs block proteins that suppress the immune system, allowing it to attack cancer cells more effectively.
Cellular therapies: This involves modifying immune cells (like T-cells) in a lab and reintroducing them to the body to target cancer.
Cancer vaccines: These vaccines stimulate the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells.
Cytokines: These are proteins that help regulate the immune system and can be used to boost its response against cancer.
Oncolytic viruses: These are viruses that are modified to infect and kill cancer cells.

list.title: Delivery methods:
list.snippet: Immunotherapy can be administered in various ways, including intravenously (IV), orally (as pills), or through injections.

list.title: Combination therapies:
list.snippet: Immunotherapy is often used in combination with other cancer treatments like chemotherapy, surgery, or radiation therapy.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, immunotherapy empowers the body's own defenses to combat cancer, offering a potentially powerful and targeted approach to cancer treatment.
